clue.text: Happy warrior a Puritan would kill, but not hang!

definitions.text: Happy warrior a Puritan would kill, but not hang!

parts.words: Happy warrior a Puritan would kill, but not hang!
parts.note: a smiling soldier of the Royalist side, the enemy of Cromwell's Puritans, who would kill him in battle but would never hang his portrait on a wall

explanation.surface: A cheerful soldier whom a Puritan would slay but never execute on the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang' reads as the gallows but means hanging a picture: Frans Hals's famous portrait shows a grinning Royalist officer, and Puritans fought the Royalists in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Frans Hals portrait of a smiling seventeenth-century officer, a Royalist of the kind Parliament's Puritans fought.

clue.text: The pest — give him beans!

parts.note: the crop-eating insect shares its name with a Mediterranean tree whose pods are sold as carob beans, so 'give him beans' is both a scolding and a menu

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry to punish some nuisance by giving him a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give him beans' sounds like 'give him a hiding', but the carob tree is called the locust tree and its pods locust beans.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarming grasshopper that strips crops is a classic plague insect, and carob pods are known as its beans.

clue.text: Publicly expose under-cover work

parts.note: reads like exposing a spy's secret work, but describes pulling the drape off a statue or plaque at an opening ceremony

explanation.surface: Revealing to the world the activities of a secret agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under-cover work' suggests espionage; it is literally a work (a statue or painting) under a cover, revealed at a ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove the covering from a new monument at a ceremony is to reveal it to the public for the first time.

clue.text: Bag like the Ark representatively

definitions.meaning: a large travelling case or carry-all
Noah's Ark took aboard a pair of every kind of creature, so it contained every species by representatives

explanation.surface: A piece of luggage compared to Noah's vessel full of sample animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase it says the ship contained every kind, two of each standing for the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A capacious travel case takes in everything, just as Noah's boat took in every animal species by pairs.

clue.text: No inferno, vulgarly speaking, but a time of merrymaking

indicators.note: a common, aitch-dropping accent says 'no hell' as 'no 'ell', which sounds like the festive word

parts.note: an inferno is hell, so 'no inferno' is 'no hell'

explanation.surface: Rather than the fires of damnation, there is a season of festivity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vulgarly speaking' is the sound signal: drop the H as a Cockney would and 'no 'ell' gives the Christmas word.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas, the feast season of carols and celebration, is called by this French-derived word.

clue.text: Is angry in the P.O. ?

definitions.meaning: ... one's feet, as someone in a temper does
what a post office sells: adhesive labels for postage

explanation.surface: Someone losing their temper at the Post Office counter.
explanation.walkthrough: P.O. is the abbreviation for Post Office.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone furious pounds a foot on the floor, and postage labels are what a post office counter sells.

clue.text: Spouters for temperance

parts.note: sounds like orators lecturing against drink, but describes china vessels with spouts that serve the abstainer's beverage

explanation.surface: Teetotal campaigners holding forth against alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spouters' are both windbags making speeches and vessels with spouts; the temperance movement promoted tea in place of alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Vessels for brewing and pouring the drink teetotallers favour, each with a spout.

clue.text: Mother making a scene when a rich patron appears !

parts.note: MA is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: the letters of the words are made into a new word, worked up into something else

explanation.surface: Mum causing a fuss when a wealthy benefactor turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a scene' reads as causing a fuss, but 'making' is the anagram signal; Maecenas was the Roman patron of Virgil and Horace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman statesman who backed Virgil and Horace gave his name to any generous sponsor of the arts.

clue.text: Left for Compton Street

definitions.meaning: in heraldry the left-hand side is the ... side
a 1913 novel by Compton Mackenzie titled with this street's name

explanation.surface: Someone heading off to a road named Compton Street.
explanation.walkthrough: Compton Mackenzie's novel 'Sinister Street' is the second sense; Old Compton Street in Soho adds the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for left came to mean ominous, and it names Compton Mackenzie's novel of youth.

clue.text: See 1 across
Do it to a ship, a road vehicle even

parts.note: a car is a road vehicle
e'en is the poetic contraction of even

explanation.surface: An instruction for treating a vessel, or else a motor car.
explanation.walkthrough: To careen a ship is to tip it on its side to clean or repair the hull.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipwrights heel a vessel over on the beach to scrape its bottom; that operation is what the clue invites you to perform.

clue.text: Substitute for money between buyer and seller

definitions.meaning: a token or chip used in place of coins in games
the shop's flat-topped table across which goods are sold

explanation.surface: Something standing in for cash in a shop transaction.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaming token stands in for cash, and the shop's long table separates customer from shopkeeper.

clue.text: Watch spring line

definitions.meaning: the coiled hairspring in a watch
a curve winding round a centre

explanation.surface: A list of watch parts: a spring and a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch's hairspring is a flat coil, and a curve winding ever outward from a centre is the same shape.

clue.text: Peers under them finding nothing but ice-creams outside

indicators.note: the ice-cream word sits around the nothing, on its outside

parts.note: cornets are ice-cream cones
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Lords who find only ice-cream cones around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peers' here are nobles, under small crowns; a British ice-cream cone is a cornet.
explanation.definitionFit: Small crowns worn by nobles below royalty, so a peer stands under one at a coronation.

clue.text: Looked up to find a penny in the mud

parts.note: d was the abbreviation for an old British penny
mired means stuck in mud

explanation.surface: Searching down in the mud to find a lost coin.
explanation.walkthrough: D stands for the pre-decimal British penny, from Latin denarius.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold someone in high regard is to respect them, so the past tense matches 'looked up to'.

clue.text: Measure of variations on the trombone?

definitions.text: Measure of variations on the trombone?

parts.words: Measure of variations on the trombone?
parts.note: a rate that rises and falls with circumstances, pictured as the slide moving up and down the notes of a trombone

explanation.surface: Musical variations played on a slide instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: A fee scale that adjusts to income is pictured by the trombone, which plays its notes by sliding.
explanation.definitionFit: A system of charges that moves up or down with some other quantity, such as income.

clue.text: A glass to Hesperus

definitions.meaning: a tall beer glass, or a large sherry glass
the ship in Longfellow's poem 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' was a two-masted sailing vessel of this type

explanation.surface: Raising a drink as a toast to the evening star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A glass to' suggests a toast; Hesperus is the evening star but here the ship in Longfellow's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall drinking vessel shares its name with a fore-and-aft rigged sailing ship like Longfellow's wrecked one.

clue.text: In the short run he is hopeful of the race

definitions.text: In the short run he is hopeful of the race

parts.words: In the short run he is hopeful of the race
parts.note: reads as someone optimistic for the short term, but describes an athlete who expects to win a dash

explanation.surface: An investor optimistic for the near term about some contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the short run' sounds like economic jargon; literally it is a short-distance race.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete who competes over short distances at full speed hopes to win the dash.

clue.text: Bonnet without strings ?

parts.note: a headgear that has no ties, and figuratively one standing for freedom from any constraint, the Phrygian cap of the French Revolution

explanation.surface: A hat lacking ribbons to tie under the chin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without strings' means both lacking ties and free of conditions; the soft red cap was the emblem of freedom in revolutionary France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phrygian cap worn by freed slaves in Rome and revolutionaries in France symbolised freedom.

clue.text: In the way of the world he may fall in a state of confusion

definitions.text: In the way of the world he

indicators.note: the words are thrown into disorder, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone in worldly affairs who may tumble into a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Way of the World' is Congreve's comedy, whose villain is Mr Fainall; 'state of confusion' rearranges FALL IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: Fainall is the scheming husband among the characters of Congreve's Restoration comedy.

clue.text: Vehicle of top people on their way to being topless

definitions.text: Vehicle of top people on their way to being topless

parts.words: Vehicle of top people on their way to being topless
parts.note: the cart carrying aristocrats to the guillotine, where they would lose their heads

explanation.surface: Transport for the upper classes heading somewhere sunny and undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' means beheaded: in the French Revolution nobles rode an open cart to the guillotine.
explanation.definitionFit: The open cart that took condemned prisoners to execution in revolutionary Paris.

clue.text: I was so spotty when small

definitions.text: I was so spotty when small

parts.words: I was so spotty when small
parts.note: reads as a childhood complaint about spots, but means the lower-case letter i carries a point over it

explanation.surface: Someone recalling a spotty childhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' is the letter and 'small' means lower case: the small letter i has a point above it.
explanation.definitionFit: Marked with points or spots, as the lower-case letter i is.

clue.text: Bee for Beer ?

parts.note: a bee is known for its sting, and an old name for a strong ale sounds as if it has that sting in it

explanation.surface: Swapping a bee for a beer, as if a typo.
explanation.walkthrough: Stingo is an old word for strong ale; a bee's mark is its sting, and a strong beer has a sting too.
explanation.definitionFit: An old name for strong, sharp-tasting ale with a kick to it.

clue.text: I'd doxies that went red with confusion

indicators.note: the words are put into confusion, a sign their letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Disreputable women who blushed in embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went red' looks like blushing but means rusted; 'with confusion' rearranges I'D DOXIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron that combines with oxygen turns reddish rust, so it has gone red through corrosion.

clue.text: Meaning I am left

parts.note: I'm is the contraction of I am
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone saying they are the one who remains.
explanation.definitionFit: The significance or sense of something, its gist.

clue.text: How a stop-order may be given

indicators.note: the letters may be given in another order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking the manner in which an order to halt is issued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be given' rearranges HOW A.
explanation.definitionFit: A command to halt, traditionally shouted to a horse.

clue.text: Hawthorne's prophetic start

definitions.note: adjective standing for a noun: the clue means 'of a prophet', the Old Testament prophet who rebuked David

indicators.note: only the beginning of the name is kept, its end cut away

parts.note: the American novelist Hawthorne's first name was Nathaniel

explanation.surface: The opening of an American novelist's work that foretells events.
explanation.walkthrough: The first six letters of Nathaniel Hawthorne's first name give the prophet who rebuked King David.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathan is the Old Testament seer who confronted King David over Bathsheba.

clue.text: Mrs. Samuel Whiskers takes on the chairman

parts.note: Samuel Whiskers is a rat in Beatrix Potter's stories, so his wife is a she-rat

explanation.surface: A character from Beatrix Potter takes on the chair of a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The chairman' is not a meeting's chair but the eighteenth-century furniture designer, famous for chairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Sheraton was the furniture designer whose name is attached to a style of chair.

clue.text: How delight visited Shelley

parts.note: Shelley's poem begins by addressing the Spirit of Delight, complaining that it comes to him seldom

explanation.surface: A question about how happiness came to the poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's lyric opens 'Rarely, rarely, comest thou, Spirit of Delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seldom, or not often, which is how the poet said delight came to him.

clue.text: Designer of London's variety theatre ?

parts.note: the London Palladium, a famous variety theatre, sounds as if it were named after the Italian Renaissance architect

explanation.surface: Asking who drew up the plans for a West End music hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The London Palladium is a famous variety theatre; the architect Andrea Palladio has nothing to do with it except the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrea Palladio was a sixteenth-century Italian architect whose classical style became Palladianism.
